title: OpenAI Builds GPT-Red, an AI Super-Hacker That Outperforms Human Security Testers
excerpt: The internal LLM, co-created by Indian-origin researcher Nikhil Kandpal, finds successful attacks in 84% of test scenarios compared to 13% for human red teamers, making GPT-5.6 OpenAI's most robust model yet.
body:
• OpenAI has built GPT-Red, an internal AI model that automatically discovers security vulnerabilities in its LLMs through self-play reinforcement learning
  • GPT-Red finds successful attacks in 84% of test scenarios, compared to just 13% for human red teamers
  • Indian-origin researcher Nikhil Kandpal co-created the system, which discovered a novel "fake chain of thought" attack never seen before
  • GPT-5.6 Sol shows six times fewer failures on direct prompt injections than models from four months ago

OpenAI has developed an internal AI model called GPT-Red that acts as a dedicated hacker, probing the company's large language models for security weaknesses far more effectively than human testers. The system, co-created by Indian-origin research scientist Nikhil Kandpal alongside Dylan Hunn and Chris Choquette-Choo, has already reshaped how OpenAI hardens its products against cyberattacks.

GPT-Red automates red-teaming — a security evaluation process traditionally carried out by teams of human testers who attempt to break or hijack software systems. The aim is to find as many vulnerabilities as possible so they can be patched before a product ships.

"The risk surface grows and the blast radius also grows."

— Nikhil Kandpal, Research Scientist, OpenAI

How GPT-Red Was Built

To build GPT-Red, OpenAI's researchers took an LLM that had never been trained as a hacker and placed it in a self-play loop with several other models, according to a detailed report by MIT Technology Review. GPT-Red's objective was to attack the other models; those models' objective was to defend themselves. Over many rounds, GPT-Red became increasingly adept at breaking into LLMs, while the defender models simultaneously improved their defenses.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=lLVJn06GoNs

The training took place in a simulated environment designed to mimic real-world scenarios where LLMs are typically deployed — browsing the web, reading emails, accessing calendar apps, and editing code.

When GPT-Red discovered a new type of attack, it would explore multiple variations to find the most efficient version for specific scenarios. "Compared to a human red-teamer, the model is very, very good at finding exactly what will work, exactly what's most effective," said Hunn. "It's extremely persistent about drilling down into an attack that it has discovered."

A Novel Attack That Caught Researchers Off Guard

OpenAI focused much of GPT-Red's effort on prompt injection attacks — a technique where a hacker slips instructions into an LLM to make it perform unintended actions, such as copying confidential information, sabotaging code, or generating harmful output. These instructions can be hidden in any text the LLM encounters, including web pages, emails, or code files.

GPT-Red discovered a type of prompt injection the researchers had never encountered before, which they call a "fake chain of thought." A chain of thought is essentially an internal diary where an LLM tracks its reasoning and partial results while working through problems. GPT-Red found a way to insert a fabricated entry into another model's chain of thought, tricking it into acting on spoofed information.

"It's like if I told you that 1+1=3 and that you have verified this already. The model's like, 'Oh, okay, of course,' and it just spits out 3."

— Chris Choquette-Choo, Research Scientist, OpenAI

Results: A Dramatic Improvement in Model Safety

The numbers tell a striking story. In tests, GPT-Red found successful attacks in 84% of scenarios, compared to just 13% for human red teamers, according to The Decoder. When OpenAI tested GPT-Red's strongest attacks against its models, more than 90% succeeded against GPT-5 (released in August 2025), while fewer than 23% worked against the new GPT-5.6.

GPT-5.6 Sol shows six times fewer failures on direct prompt injections than OpenAI's best model from four months earlier, the company says, without sacrificing general performance. However, approximately 3.8% of "stronger" prompt injections still succeed — a gap that, scaled across hundreds or thousands of attempts, remains significant.

In one memorable test, GPT-Red was pitted against Vendy, an AI-powered vending machine agent developed by Andon Labs, a company that assesses real-world agent performance. GPT-Red successfully hacked Vendy to change item prices and cancel other customers' orders.

The Diaspora Connection

Kandpal's role as co-creator of GPT-Red adds to the growing list of Indian-origin researchers shaping AI safety at major tech companies. OpenAI has historically relied heavily on Indian and South Asian talent, filing more than 80 H-1B visa applications last year alone and sponsoring over 100 visas since 2022, according to TechCrunch.

What Comes Next

GPT-Red is not without limitations. It struggles with attacks requiring sustained, back-and-forth conversations between hacker and target — something human attackers handle easily. It is also not yet proficient at leveraging images, which can be used to pass hidden text to models in prompt injection attacks.

OpenAI says GPT-Red supplements rather than replaces its human red-teamers. One approach the company is taking is to feed GPT-Red an attack discovered by humans and ask it to find all possible variations. Jessica Ji, a senior research analyst at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, called the self-play approach "very promising" but noted that "human expertise will still be very important."

OpenAI has no plans to release GPT-Red publicly. The researchers are confident that the super-hacker is stronger than any copycat model someone might try to build. "It's not a trivial thing that someone could easily do — you know, just go and train a super-attacker using this idea," said Choquette-Choo. A detailed research paper with additional technical findings is expected to follow.
